name: Yoruba
blurb: People of the talking drum, whose dùndún speaks the tonal language word for word and whose Ife casters shaped some of Africa's finest bronzes.
intro: The Yoruba are one of West Africa's largest peoples, settled for more than a thousand years in the forests and savannahs of what is now south-western Nigeria, Benin and Togo. Theirs is a civilisation of cities — Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the spiritual cradle, Ọ̀yọ́, Ìbàdàn, Abẹ́òkúta — each ruled by an ọba beneath a beaded crown. Yorùbá is a tonal language, and on the dùndún talking drum that tonality becomes speech: a master drummer can make the drum recite a proverb or call a person's praise-name across a market square. The world knows them too for the towering Egúngún masquerade that brings the ancestors among the living, for àdìre indigo-dyed cloth, and for the Ife bronze and terracotta heads whose serene naturalism astonished the museums of Europe.
respect: Engage with Yoruba-led cultural organisations, artists and master crafts­people, learn from them directly, credit makers fairly, and never share sacred or restricted material.

name: Native Hawaiian (Kānaka Maoli)
blurb: Voyagers of the open Pacific whose hula dances the chant, and whose wayfinders read the stars without instruments.
intro: The Kānaka Maoli are the Native people of Hawaiʻi, descendants of Polynesian navigators who crossed thousands of kilometres of open ocean by double-hulled canoe more than a thousand years ago. Their knowledge is voiced in oli (chant) and danced in hula, which does not merely accompany the words but embodies them — every hand a wave, a rain, an ancestor. Wayfinders still cross the Pacific guided only by stars, swell and bird, as the canoe Hōkūleʻa has proved to the world. After a century in which ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi was nearly silenced, language and arts are in determined revival.

name: Zulu
blurb: People of the heavens whose isicathamiya harmonies, indlamu stamp and beadwork carry the word.
intro: The amaZulu — the people of the heavens — are the largest cultural nation of South Africa, heirs of the chieftaincies that Shaka forged into a kingdom in the early 1800s. Their world is carried in isiZulu, a tonal Nguni language rich in click sounds and praise; in the close a-cappella harmonies of isicathamiya; in the thundering stamp of indlamu; and in beadwork so precise that a string of coloured beads — an ucu, a 'love-letter' — can be read like a sentence.

name: Mapuche
blurb: People of the land of southern Chile and Argentina — the kultrún drum, ñimin weaving and the silver of the trapelakucha.
intro: The Mapuche are the people of the land — che, the people, of mapu, the land — of south-central Chile and the Andean steppe of Argentina. They never fell to the Inca and held the Spanish at the Biobío river for three centuries, keeping their freedom until the late 1800s. Their world is voiced in ülkantun song over the kultrún drum and the long trutruca horn, woven into the ñimin patterns of the loom, and worked in the silver of the trapelakucha worn at a woman's breast. They speak Mapudungun, the speech of the land, carried for most of its life in voice alone.

name: Balinese
epithet: People of the Island of the Gods
blurb: People of the island of a thousand temples, whose gamelan, legong and barong turn daily life into living offering.
intro: The Balinese are the people of Bali, a small Hindu island in a vast Muslim-majority archipelago, whose faith — Agama Hindu Dharma — fills the calendar with ritual. Life turns on the banjar, the neighbourhood council, and on a ceaseless rhythm of offering: the canang sari laid out each dawn, the temple odalan, the great processions to the sea. Art is not set apart from worship — the shimmering bronze of the gamelan, the trembling fingers and darting eyes of the legong, the carved demon-king Barong and the chattering chorus of the kecak are all addressed, first, to the gods.

name: Maya
epithet: Keepers of the Count and the Loom
blurb: Living heirs of the Long Count and the Popol Vuh — weavers of the huipil whose marimba still carries the village square.
intro: The Maya are not a people of the past but some seven million living people across Guatemala, southern Mexico and northern Central America — the descendants of the civilisation that raised Tikal and Chichén Itzá, kept the Long Count calendar, and wrote the Popol Vuh. They speak around thirty Mayan languages, terrace the volcanic highlands for maize, weave the huipil on the backstrap loom, and gather to the marimba in the village square.
respect: Engage with Maya-led weaving cooperatives and language organisations, buy textiles directly and fairly from the weavers, and respect that some ceremony and knowledge is restricted.

name: Sámi
blurb: Reindeer-herders of the Arctic whose joik can sing a person, an animal or a place into being.
intro: The Sámi are the indigenous people of Sápmi, the Arctic reaches of northern Europe. For thousands of years they have herded reindeer, crafted duodji, and sung joik — a vocal tradition that does not sing about a person or place, but sings the thing itself into the room.
respect: Learn from Sámi institutions and artists, respect that joik and duodji belong to their communities, and support language revitalisation. FirstCiv keeps such recordings community-owned and consent-first.

name: Māori
blurb: Tangata whenua of Aotearoa — haka, waiata and whakairo carving carrying ancestral memory.
intro: The Māori are the tangata whenua — the people of the land — of Aotearoa, descendants of Polynesian navigators who crossed the open Pacific by waka some eight centuries ago. Their world is held in whakapapa (genealogy that binds people to mountains, rivers and ancestors), voiced in haka and waiata, and carved into the wood of the wharenui in whakairo. After a long colonial eclipse, te reo Māori and its arts are in determined revival.
respect: Engage with Māori-led organisations and iwi, learn te reo, and respect that taonga (treasures) carry mana and belong to their people.

name: Maasai
blurb: Pastoralists of the Rift Valley whose adumu dance and beadwork encode age, status and lineage.
intro: The Maasai are semi-nomadic pastoralists of the Great Rift Valley, herding cattle, goats and sheep across the open grasslands that straddle the border of Kenya and Tanzania. Their lives turn on the herd and on the age-set system, by which boys become moran — the warriors who once guarded the cattle — and in time become elders. The world knows them by the adumu, the soaring jumping dance, by the deep red shúkà cloth, and by beadwork whose every colour and pattern speaks of age, status and lineage. They speak Maa, a Nilotic tongue carried entirely in voice and memory.

name: Tuvan
blurb: Herders of the steppe who sing two notes at once, echoing wind, river and animal.
intro: The Tuvans are a Turkic people of the south-Siberian steppe and taiga, herders of horse, sheep, yak and reindeer at the very centre of Asia, where the Yenisei is born. Their gift to the world is khöömei — throat-singing, in which a single voice splits into two or more notes at once, drawing a deep drone beneath a whistling overtone melody that imitates wind over grass, water over stone and the call of an animal. The igil and doshpuluur carry the same sound on horsehair strings. Their world is held between Tengrism and shamanism, the spirit of every spring and mountain, and a deep-rooted Tibetan Buddhism.
respect: Support Tuvan musicians and khöömei masters directly, learn a few words of the Tuvan language, and back community-led recording.

name: Ainu
blurb: Indigenous people of the north whose yukar epics were sung for nights without end.
intro: The Ainu are the Indigenous people of the northern islands — Ainu Mosir, 'the quiet land of human beings' — across Hokkaidō, Sakhalin and the Kurils. They are fishers of salmon and hunters of deer and bear, whose world is alive with kamuy, the spirits who dwell in every animal, plant, river and fire. Their inheritance is carried in the upopo round-songs sung seated in a circle, in the yukar epics that once filled whole winter nights, in the breath of the mukkuri mouth-harp, and in the bold moreu spirals embroidered onto attus elm-bark robes. The Ainu language — a true isolate, kin to no other on Earth — is critically endangered, yet a determined revival is under way.
respect: Support Ainu-led cultural organisations and the Upopoy National Ainu Museum in Hokkaidō; learn and share accurate history; buy attus weaving and woodcarving directly from Ainu makers; and back language-revival programmes. On FirstCiv, recordings are made only with the consent of Ainu keepers, ownership stays with the community of origin, and royalties flow back to them — so that the culture sustains the people who keep it alive.

name: Quechua
epithet: People of the Sun and the Loom
blurb: Heirs of the Andes whose textiles read like books and whose music climbs the mountains.
intro: The Quechua are the heirs of the Andes — the largest family of Indigenous peoples in the Americas, descendants of the herders, farmers and weavers whose lands the Inca once knit into Tawantinsuyu, the realm of the four quarters. They speak Runa Simi, the people's tongue, terrace the steep mountainsides for maize and a thousand potatoes, and weave textiles so dense with meaning that a cloth can be read like a page. Their huayno songs, pan-pipes and the small charango carry the same memory in sound.

name: Tuareg
blurb: People of the veil whose Tifinagh script and desert blues cross the dunes.
intro: The Tuareg — who call themselves the Kel Tamasheq, 'those who speak Tamasheq' — are a Berber people of the central Sahara and Sahel, scattered across Mali, Niger, Algeria, Libya and Burkina Faso. For more than two thousand years they have crossed the desert by camel, guiding the salt and gold caravans between the oases and the Sahel. The men, not the women, wear the indigo tagelmust veil whose dye once rubbed off onto the skin, earning the Tuareg their old nickname, the 'blue people'. Theirs is a society with strong matrilineal threads, an ancient written script — Tifinagh — and a desert music, assouf, that has carried their longing for home onto stages around the world.
respect: Support Tuareg-led cultural associations and artisan cooperatives — especially the inadan silversmiths and the women who keep the imzad and Tifinagh alive — and buy crafts such as the Cross of Agadez directly from their makers.

name: Inuit
blurb: People of the sea ice whose katajjaq is a breath-game sung face to face.
intro: The Inuit are the people of the circumpolar Arctic, from Chukotka across Alaska and Arctic Canada to Greenland. For millennia they have read the sea ice, built the iglu, hunted from the qajaq, and traded the long polar night for song. Katajjaq — a breath-game sung face to face between two women — ends, always, in laughter.

name: Aboriginal Australians
epithet: The Oldest Living Cultures on Earth
blurb: The oldest continuous cultures on Earth, mapping the land in Songlines 65,000 years deep.
intro: Aboriginal Australians are the First Peoples of the Australian continent, with an unbroken presence reaching back at least 65,000 years — the oldest continuous living cultures on Earth. They are not one people but hundreds of distinct nations, each with its own Country, language and Law. Knowledge is carried in Songlines that thread across the land, in the deep yiḏaki drone, in ceremony, and in painting that maps the Dreaming.
respect: Follow Aboriginal leadership, never share sacred or restricted material, and ensure recordings are made with the consent of Traditional Owners — which is how FirstCiv operates.

name: Hmong
blurb: Highland weavers whose paj ntaub story-cloths stitch migration and memory.
intro: The Hmong are a highland people whose home is the misted ridge-tops of southern China and the borderlands of Vietnam, Laos and Thailand — and, since the wars of the twentieth century, a far-flung diaspora that reaches deep into the United States, France and Australia. They reckon themselves not by nation but by clan, and carry their history not in books but in cloth: the paj ntaub, the 'flower cloth', whose appliqué and cross-stitch once held a script lost to conquest, and whose story-cloths now stitch whole journeys of flight and exile into a single panel. Their courtship songs answer one another across the New Year field, the reed-piped qeej speaks to the dead, and indigo batik draws cosmology in beeswax and dye.
respect: By recording and sharing it with consent and with credit and benefit flowing back to the community.

name: San
epithet: The First People of the Kalahari
blurb: Among humanity's oldest lineages, whose click languages and trance dance still heal.
intro: The San are the first people of southern Africa — hunter-gatherers of the Kalahari whose ancestors have lived on this land for tens of thousands of years, carrying some of the oldest genetic lineages of humankind. They are not one people but many, speaking a family of click languages — among the most sound-rich tongues on Earth — and bound together by the trance-dance, in which healers enter altered states to draw sickness from the sick. Their hand painted the eland onto rock across the subcontinent. Dispossessed of much of their land and pressed hard by the modern world, the San endure, and their knowledge endures with them.
respect: Recording elders' speech, songs and stories with their consent fixes endangered click languages before they fall silent, and supporting San-led community trusts, land claims and language schools keeps that knowledge in San hands.

name: Gnawa
epithet: Keepers of the Night of Healing
blurb: Descendants of sub-Saharan lineages whose all-night lila summons healing and trance.
intro: The Gnawa are a Moroccan people and spiritual brotherhood descended from the enslaved sub-Saharan Africans — Bambara, Hausa, Fulani and others — carried north across the Sahara over centuries. From that wound they wove a culture of healing: the lila, an all-night ceremony of music, incense and trance led by a maâlem on the deep, three-string guembri lute, driven by the iron clatter of the qraqeb castanets and sung in a Darija laced with remembered Bambara. Colour by colour the night summons the mluk, the spirits, until the afflicted dance their pain into release. Inscribed by UNESCO in 2019, Gnawa music now fills festival stages from Essaouira to the world — yet its heart remains the brotherhood and the long night.
respect: Support the maâlems and brotherhoods directly — attend their ceremonies and festivals on their terms, buy their recordings, and respect that the sacred core of the lila is not for sale or spectacle.

name: Tibetan
blurb: People of the high plateau whose overtone chant and thangka hold a vast inner cosmology.
intro: The Tibetans are the people of the world's highest plateau — a roof of grassland, glacier and thin bright air ringed by the Himalaya. For more than a thousand years their lives have turned around the dharma: the deep overtone chant of the Gyütö monks, the patient brilliance of thangka scroll-painting, the sand mandala built and swept away in a single breath, and the prayer flags and mani stones that set the wind itself to praying. Theirs is a culture that holds a vast inner cosmology lightly, in everyday hands.
respect: Support Tibetan-led monasteries, thangka schools, language nests and cultural institutes; learn a little of the language and its etiquette; buy art and crafts directly from Tibetan makers; and back ethical, consent-based archives. On FirstCiv, every recording is made with the keepers' consent, ownership stays with the community of origin, and royalties flow back to them — while sacred or restricted material is never recorded.

name: Diné (Navajo)
epithet: The People of the Glittering World
blurb: Weavers and singers of the Southwest whose chantways restore hózhó — beauty and balance.
intro: The Diné — known to the world as the Navajo — are the largest Native nation in the United States, holding a homeland of high desert and red rock bounded by four sacred mountains. Their world turns on hózhó, the state of beauty, harmony and balance that the great Chantways are sung to restore. They are master weavers, whose rugs read like maps of the land, and silver-and-turquoise smiths whose work the world now wears. Life is lived around the hogan, the round earth-and-timber dwelling whose door faces the rising sun.
respect: Support it on the People's own terms: buy weaving and silverwork directly from Diné artists rather than imitations, back Diné bizaad immersion schools and language programmes, and respect that ceremonies and sandpaintings are sacred and not for public sale.

name: Mongolian
epithet: Nomads of the Eternal Blue Sky
blurb: Nomads of the steppe whose urtiin duu stretches a single line across the whole horizon.
intro: The Mongolians are the nomads of the great steppe, herders who for three thousand years have followed their horses, sheep and camels across the grasslands beneath Tengri, the eternal blue sky. From the ger they read weather and pasture; in the saddle they cross a horizon that seems to have no edge. Their voices answer that vastness — urtiin duu, the long-song, stretches a single line of melody clear across the plain, the morin khuur carries the gait of a galloping horse, and khöömii lets one throat sound two notes at once. Each summer Naadam gathers the 'three manly games' of wrestling, archery and horse-racing.
respect: Support the herding communities and musicians who keep the traditions living — learn the long-song, the morin khuur or the vertical Mongol bichig script through Mongolian-led schools and ensembles, and back climate and pasture programmes, since the worsening dzud winters threaten the nomadic way of life. On FirstCiv you can contribute or collect consented recordings, with royalties flowing back to the community of origin.

name: Yanomami
epithet: Forest People of the Falling Sky
blurb: Forest people of the Amazon whose shamanic songs name every spirit of the canopy.
intro: The Yanomami are one of the largest relatively isolated forest peoples of the Amazon, living in some hundreds of communities scattered across the highlands where Brazil meets Venezuela. They dwell in the shabono — a great ring of palm-thatched roof enclosing a single communal clearing — and read the forest as a library of plants, animals and weather. Their world is held together by the xapiri, the luminous spirit-beings called down by shamans who inhale the yãkoana snuff, and renewed at the reahu, the funerary feast that lays the dead to rest and binds allies together. As the shaman and author Davi Kopenawa warns, the sky itself could fall if the forest and its keepers are not protected — and today illegal gold-mining brings mercury, disease and violence to their land.
